en: To encourage or assist someone in doing something wrong
hook: ABET: placing A BET on the criminal and helping him win.
story: The driver didn't rob the bank himself, but he waited outside with the engine running and drove the robbers away. The court found him guilty of aiding and abetting. To abet is to help or encourage wrongdoing. Remember the legal phrase: aid and abet.

en: Easy to reach, use, obtain, or understand
hook: ACCESSIBLE: easy ACCESS.
story: The new metro made central Dhaka accessible from Uttara in thirty minutes. The professor's book is accessible too; even high school students can follow it. Accessible means easy to reach or understand. Buildings with ramps are accessible to wheelchair users.

en: Excessively eager to acquire money or possessions
hook: ACQUISITIVE: always ACQUIRING more.
story: The acquisitive businessman bought land, factories, and shopping malls, yet he always wanted more: one more building, one more company. Acquisitive means greedy for possessions. Synonyms: avaricious, covetous, rapacious.

en: To combine or unite into one
hook: AMALGAMATE: A MALL that GATHERs many shops into one.
story: Two small banks amalgamated to form one large bank, combining their branches, staff, and customers. Amalgamate means to merge into a single whole. Dentists once used an amalgam, a mix of metals, for fillings.

en: To reduce the force, effect, or value of; to make thin
hook: ATTENUATE: makes it THIN, TENUOUS.
story: Thick curtains attenuated the noise from the street, turning the honking into a soft hum. Some vaccines use attenuated viruses, weakened so they can't cause disease. To attenuate is to weaken or reduce. Synonyms: diminish, dilute.

en: To make greater by adding to
hook: AUGMENT: like AUGMENTED reality adding layers to the world.
story: Nadia augmented her small salary by tutoring three students in the evenings. Her income grew by forty percent. To augment is to increase or enhance by adding. Augmented reality adds digital images to what you see.

en: A strong dislike or disinclination
hook: AVERSION: you AVERT (turn away) your eyes from it.
story: Rafi has an aversion to public speaking. His palms sweat and his voice shakes even at a small meeting. An aversion is a strong dislike. Many children have an aversion to vegetables; many investors have an aversion to risk.

en: Cheerfully carefree; casually indifferent to something serious
hook: BLITHE: BLISSfully unaware.
story: With exams one day away, Tanvir was blithely playing cricket, as if nothing mattered. His mother couldn't believe his blithe attitude. Blithe means carefree and lighthearted, sometimes in a careless way. Blithe disregard for safety is dangerous.

en: The feeling that someone or something is worthless or beneath consideration
hook: CONTEMPT: CON + TEMPT; you're not even tempted to respect it.
story: The rich man looked at the street vendor with contempt, as if he weren't even human. In court, the man who insulted the judge was charged with contempt of court. Contempt means disdain, a feeling that something is worthless.

en: To waste time; to be slow
hook: DAWDLE: like a DOODLE, wasting time drawing nothing.
story: Mitu's little brother dawdled on the way to school: watching ants, chasing butterflies, chatting with the tea seller. He arrived thirty minutes late. To dawdle is to move slowly and waste time. Synonyms: linger, dilly-dally.

en: To cause something to change direction; to avoid
bn: বিচ্যুত করা; ভিন্ন দিকে ফিরিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: DEFLECT: like a shield DEFLECTING an arrow.
story: The goalkeeper deflected the shot over the bar with his fingertips. Later, when reporters asked about his team's poor defense, the coach deflected the question by praising the fans. To deflect is to turn aside, physically or in conversation.

en: To regard as unimportant or untrustworthy; to disregard
hook: GRE trick: DISCOUNT means to ignore, not just lower the price.
story: Scientists at first discounted the young researcher's findings because she was unknown. Later, they realized she was right. On the GRE, to discount means to disregard or dismiss as unreliable. Don't discount small daily study sessions; they add up.

en: A person who opposes official policy, especially of an authoritarian state
hook: DIS-SIDE-ent: on the other SIDE.
story: The dissident writer criticized the government in her novels and was jailed for years. Her books were banned, but they were secretly copied and passed hand to hand. A dissident openly opposes those in power. Synonym: dissenter.

en: Successful in producing the desired result; effective
hook: EFFICACIOUS: EFFECTIVE.
story: Oral saline, a simple mix of salt, sugar, and water, proved remarkably efficacious against diarrhea, saving millions of lives. Efficacious means effective. The efficacy of a medicine is how well it works.

en: Fair and impartial
hook: EQUITABLE: EQUAL for all.
story: When their father passed away, the three siblings divided the land in an equitable way, each receiving a fair share after much discussion. Equitable means fair and just. An equitable system treats everyone fairly, not necessarily identically.

en: Not regular or predictable; inconsistent
hook: ERRATIC: full of ERRORS, all over the place.
story: The old bus had erratic brakes; sometimes they worked perfectly, sometimes they barely worked at all. Rafi's study habits were erratic too: ten hours one day, nothing for a week. Erratic means unpredictable and irregular.

en: Hardworking and diligent
hook: INDUSTRIOUS: works like a whole INDUSTRY.
story: The industrious tailor worked from dawn to midnight, sewing dresses for Eid. In ten years, his single sewing machine grew into a shop with twenty workers. Industrious means hardworking. Synonyms: diligent, assiduous, sedulous.

en: To give information to; also, to give an essential quality to or influence
bn: জানানো; প্রভাবিত করা, বৈশিষ্ট্য দান করা
hook: GRE trick: experience INFORMS art means it SHAPES it from within.
story: Nadia's childhood in a fishing village informs all her paintings: rivers, boats, and nets appear in every canvas. On the GRE, inform often means to shape or deeply influence, not just to tell. Her life experience informs her art.

en: Irritating; annoying
hook: IRKSOME: something that IRKS you.
story: The irksome neighbor played loud music every night at midnight, ignoring every polite request to turn it down. Irksome means annoying and tiresome. Filling out the same form three times is irksome too.

en: A metal band for chaining someone's hands; to restrain
hook: MAN-ACLE: shackles on a MAN's hands (manus).
story: The prisoner was led into court in manacles, his hands chained together. Figuratively, Arif felt manacled by debt; he couldn't make any life choices freely. A manacle is a handcuff or chain. As a verb, to manacle is to shackle or restrain.

en: Humble about one's achievements; moderate in size or amount
hook: MODEST: MODERATE, not boastful, not extreme.
story: Despite winning a national award, the scientist was modest: 'It was my team's work, not mine.' She lived in a modest flat and earned a modest salary. Modest means humble, or not large. A modest increase is a small one.

en: Harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
hook: NOXIOUS: like NOX, toxic gas.
story: Black smoke from the brick kilns filled the air with noxious fumes; villagers coughed and crops withered. Noxious means harmful or poisonous. A noxious smell can make you sick. The opposite is innocuous.

en: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually or subtly
hook: PERNICIOUS: slowly PERISHING you.
story: Social media comparison has a pernicious effect on young people's self-esteem: slowly, quietly, they start believing they're not good enough. Pernicious means harmful in a gradual, hidden way. Pernicious rumors spread damage before anyone notices.

en: A difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation
hook: PREDICAMENT: a PREDICTION gone wrong, now you're stuck.
story: Sara found herself in a predicament: her wallet was stolen in a foreign city, her phone was dead, and she didn't speak the language. Predicament means a difficult situation that's hard to get out of. Synonyms: plight, dilemma, quandary.

en: Competent and skilled in an activity or area of knowledge
hook: PROFICIENT: as skilled as a PRO.
story: After two years of practice, Tanvir became proficient in Python; he could build a website, analyze data, and automate boring tasks. Proficient means skilled through practice. Many universities require English proficiency scores.

en: Using too many words; tediously lengthy
hook: PROLIX: PRO at being LONG.
story: The prolix speaker went on for two hours, repeating every point three times. When he finally stopped, half the audience was asleep. Prolix means tediously wordy. Synonyms: verbose, long-winded. The opposite is laconic or pithy.

en: Strong contempt; to reject with contempt
hook: SCORN: SCORE zero on respect.
story: When Arif suggested a new idea in the meeting, his senior laughed with scorn: 'What would a junior know?' Months later, his idea saved the project. Scorn means contempt; to scorn is to reject something as worthless. Synonyms: disdain, derision.

en: Lower in rank or importance; to treat as less important
hook: SUB-ORDINATE: ranked (ordered) BELOW.
story: A good manager treats her subordinates with respect, listening to junior staff as carefully as to senior executives. Subordinate means lower in rank or importance. As a verb, to subordinate is to place something below another priority: she subordinated her own comfort to her children's needs.

en: Not proper or appropriate; in bad taste
hook: UN-SEEMLY: doesn't SEEM right.
story: The guests at the funeral began an unseemly argument over the dead man's property, right next to the coffin. Everyone was embarrassed. Unseemly means improper and in bad taste. Synonyms: indecorous, unbecoming.

en: Real; used to emphasize that a description is accurate
hook: VERITABLE: VERY TRUE (veritas = truth).
story: Grandma's kitchen during Eid was a veritable factory: ten pots cooking, five people chopping, and a hundred samosas on the table. Veritable emphasizes that a description, often a metaphor, is truly fitting. A veritable genius is a real genius.
